Uprooting and Replanting the Vegetal Body of Silas Marner in George Eliot’s Silas Marner Caitlin Anderson Auburn University, Auburn Introduction Both the body and actions of George Eliot’s titular character are a source of “half-fearful fascination” in the first pages of Silas Marner (Eliot 1–2). His intimacy with his loom as well as his intimacy with the gold coins he earns for his weaving have been noted as a reflection of his “perverse” desires which must be redirected toward the formation of family (Nunokawa 274). Jeff Nunokawa suggests that this fondling of coins speaks to a masturbatory homosexuality that is made straight and external when the coins are replaced by Eppie’s hair. The straightening of Silas Marner, however, also takes place through his relationship with things that are less straightfor­ wardly inanimate and which complicate and challenge the process of sexual discipline itself. Indeed, Silas’s intimacy with plants, his love of collecting them, for example, suggests that a queer ecology is operative in Eliot’s novel and that plant bodies endow the miser with not just two, but three bodies to love: his own through the fondling of gold, Eppie’s through the fondling of her hair, and plants through the fondling of their vegetal bodies. Silas Marner, a competent healer through the use of medical herbs, is queered and treated as someone performing magic for his healing abilities which transform the bodies of plants into his “stuff,” a material which suggests that as the miser fondles gold, alchemically turning it into a body, he also transforms the bodies of plants which then may enter other bodies. As Stacey Alaimo suggests, this “transcorporeal” connection with “stuff” sug­ gests the fine line between plant and human bodies, an affinity between which Eliot suggests is insufficiently distinctive and must be eradicated (Alaimo 237). To make matters more complex, Silas’ herbal intimacy came to him through his mother. Her status as a village wise woman introduced Silas to a kinship between plants and people. His intimacy with the lively bodies of plants, freely gathered and distilled into “Marner’s stuff,” must also then be forsaken for the miser to enter into a properly domesticated Victorian modernity (7). This shift comes at a high ecological price. Alongside its mythologizing of the Victorian family, Silas Marner mythologizes the loss of the potency of plants, biodiversity, and plant literacy as part of a historical plot which naturalizes the disappearance of human intimacy with plants and even their agency itself. Indeed, as Eliot critiques Marner’s self-love, she describes his sexual anarchy as the “loam” in which the “seeds of desire are planted,” suggesting not just the potency of Marner’s dangerously hybrid thoughts, but the anarchic and agentic “nature” of plants themselves which may grow against the grain of heteronormative reproductivity (15). As contemporary ecocriticism and critical plant studies increasingly seek to explore how plant life, long considered inferior, non-agentic, and a background or instrument to human culture, may have shaped the latter, new considerations of old standards like Silas Marner may demonstrate how nineteenth-century ecologies, systems of thought which determine the use, treatment, or preservation of more-than-human life, naturalize hetero­ normative projects such as industrialized capitalism (Williams). Indeed, as Michael Marder suggests, deploying a “vegetal” lens may usefully challenge the latter and reveal more than human, more than sexual sameness as well as inter-species hybridities, long recognized in language and culture, but rarely confronted (“Resist Like a Plant” 24). Studying such recognitions, awkward moments of recognition between species may allow ecocriticism to shift the boundaries between people and plants which allow for the abuse of the latter (Marder, “What is Plant Thinking?” 124). Reading plants in Silas Marner then connects the logic of past and present deforestations and cultural defoliation to the project of modernity. Plant-based examinations of historical literature can provide a “voice of freshness” as well as a context for understanding the rarely acknowledged intimacy between plants and people then and now (Marder, “On the Vegetal Verge” 145). In this way, Eliot’s Silas Marner and the culture it reflects as plants are pushed to the side in favor of a more austere and human-centric culture allow contem­ porary scholarship to imagine new connections and intimacies which, like the miser’s more hybridized body, threaten the ecological “proprieties” of modernity. George Eliot’s writing of such proprieties provides a unique opportunity to examine how they align with modernity and become common sense in con­ temporary ecologies. Silas Marner in particular seems exceptionally concerned with acknowledging what could be considered archaic ways of thinking in order to disprove them and move them aside in favor of more modern and, for the era Eliot wrote in, progressive thought. In many cases, these archaic ways of thinking are more ecological or vegetal ways of thinking. Elizabeth Carolyn Miller suggests that Eliot’s Mill on the Floss uses a “temporally doubled methodology” in which Eliot’s temporal shifts create a story which exists in both the past and the present, the mill’s power source of either water or steam 2 C. ANDERSON

defining the timelines but also connecting them through their ecological presence (86). With the narrator of the novel “poised between the future and the past” and capable of “reading them in relation to one another,” the impact of the cultural shift from water to steam power is read through the action of the novel (Miller 94). Power, industry, and technology advance, but the presence of the flood supports a dual temporality that allows the novel to exist in both in the past and the novel’s present. Alicia Carroll explores a similar tension in Adam Bede wherein the “improvement” of the estate serves to obfuscate an ecological violence which leads to an “end to sustainable local practices through the devastation of local villages” (“‘This is a Sacred Grove’” 188). Improvement is a modernization which, as Carroll points out, Eliot seems to imagine as sustainable but which, through closer examination. represents a “masculinist green capitalism” which benefits a masculine and capitalist society and not the environment itself, a convenient privileging of masculinity in a novel with a notoriously homosocial plot (Carroll, “‘This is a Sacred Grove’” 195). Poised in that historical novel between traditional sustainable agriculture and industrialized modernity, Eliot imagines plants as anarchic beings which must be disciplined to serve the latter. Eliot’s potential as an author well aware of the anarchic power of plants is displayed again in Doreen Thireauf’s recent exploration of a potential abortion plot hidden within the subterfuge of Middlemarch. In Eliot’s Middlemarch notebook, Thierauf discovers a brief mention of the abortifacient “enringo root” plant and finds the plant provides further evidence of the novel’s codified represen­ tation of abortion couched in terms of Rosamund’s miscarriage. Thierauf points out that this mention displays the “existence of sub-public Victorian archives of knowledge,” such as the agentic nature of plants in women’s reproductive lives (488). Such discussions, like Sophie D. Christman’s discussion of “moral sym­ pathy” toward ecological life, suggest Eliot’s clear interest in the intimacy of human life with more than human life, making her work increasingly implicated in the dispersal of Victorian ecologies (81). Regulating plant life in dual temporalities of past and present, Eliot also regulates the body of Silas Marner, calling his gender in the novel into question. A hybridized figure, Silas Marner straddles the old and the new as he straddles genders, becoming a holdout for herbal medicine against the coming modernization and indus­ trialization of medicine. Within Silas Marner this modernizing seems bene­ volent and is used to obfuscate the ecological violence of industrial growth. Marner’s happiness in the novel comes only when he turns away from old ways of thinking. While his gendering remains potentially transgressive, the recovering herbalist Silas Marner represents an awareness of past thought but a purposeful movement toward a culture which divests itself particularly from medicinal plants, resettling these into inert positions in the margins of human life. WOMEN’S STUDIES 3

Altered bodies Once a healer, Silas Marner is initially tied to a traditional women’s culture by medicinal plants and queered by them as his plant treatments erode boundaries between people and things. Muddled with his mother in what Eliot presents as a feminine role, Silas’s gender seems as unstable as his treatments are volatile. Silas remembers, for example, both the knowledge and the emotional connections herbs mediated when he recalls “the relief his mother had found from a simple preparation of foxglove” (Eliot 15). This emotional connection between Silas and his medical knowledge furthers intimacy between genders and shifts gendered ontological divisions in which men are rational rather than emotional, productive rather than repro­ ductive or caring. Eroding these binaries, herbs appear to facilitate relational becoming rather than essential being; mother and son, plants and people become themselves through relation rather than essence. As Deleuze and Guattari argue, reading this intimacy as a part of “a chain of beings perpe­ tually imitating one another, progressively and regressively,” gives plants and people the same status, both sharing a horizontal ecosystem of becoming (235). To explain becoming, Deleuze and Guattari use the image of an orchid which forms part of its flower to look like a wasp so that wasps are drawn in to the flower in order to pollinate them and lead to floral reproduction. By mimicking the shape of a wasp, “the orchid deterritorializes” its own body; meanwhile, the wasp is also “deterritorialized, becoming a piece in the orchid’s reproductive apparatus” (10). The wasp and the orchid remain “heterogeneous elements,” but the act of mimicking the wasp means that the orchid is “becoming-wasp” and when the wasp is drawn in by the flower and aids in pollination, it is “becoming-orchid” (10). The wasp and the orchid have, genetically speaking, “nothing to do with each other,” and yet they have evolved together to create a relationship in which their lines of physical territory are blurred and their biological differences seem to dema­ terialize due to the ways they have become alike (10). This developed realization of becoming serves to express what the concept suggests: an ecological and biological potential for disconnected bodies to become one another. In the case of Silas Marner, it is the plants which become human as they are active agents with the ability to affect the human heart through both Silas’s intimacy with his mother gained through shared knowledge and memory, and the agentic power of the plant foxglove to regulate her heart­ beat. Meanwhile, Silas may playfully experience becoming plant himself, thriving in the lush fields and “wandering” among vegetal bodies, apart from the idea of production associated with industrialized capitalism (Eliot 7). Indeed, Silas’s foraging deepens this horizontal relationship with plants. While “wandering in the fields” (Eliot 7), Silas develops a closeness with 4 C. ANDERSON

plants that is both material and emotionally memorial. Once he has given up the practice, he finds himself looking at the way the flowers “lay on his palm,” the act bringing “crowding remembrances” (131). Silas is, in these moments, becoming plant as the plants physically surround him in the fields but also permeate his already queered body and lineage. If Silas’ herbal knowledge is “inherited from his mother,” then not only is his gender unseated through his identity relying heavily on a female figure, but so too is his genetics unseated from the human as plant knowledge becomes a genetic inheritance, his inherited traits becoming plant as the plants become human, gaining an agentic role in the novel as associating with them so deeply shapes Silas’ identity. It is worth nothing again that Silas engages in “wandering,” an act without a definition of time or space and one which takes place in fields of herbs. Silas’s foraging points out his dependency on vegetal life which feeds him both spiritually and physically. This is another moment of becoming for the herbs, their identity and agency requiring a commitment of both time and body from Silas. They demand of him his bodily presence. By drawing him out into the fields, the plants also are a part of a greater vegetal body in nature, a piece of the becoming of the fields as Silas wanders through them in search of aid. They are human as they call for his attention and time, drawing him into the fields where he can become plant and immerse himself in the vegetation in search of plants he can partner with in order to heal (Grieve 213, 325). Eliot’s naming of these plants as “fox-glove and dandelion and coltsfoot,” each of its leaves named for its association with animals, a fox’s glove, a lion’s tooth, a colt’s foot, allows the reader to remember the intimacy between living things, share in Silas’s plant literacy, and remember plants’ distinct forms and properties. Silas’ act of collecting herbs gives the plants power through their names. He does not spend his hours in the fields seeking out specific and uncommon plants that must be searched for extensively. Instead, he uses three abundantly common plants that grow wild in England. Dandelion, in particular, is so common and prolific a plant that it is and was considered an invasive weed to domestic gardeners. Coltsfoot, a common and sometimes considered invasive plant that is also a “demulcent, expectorant and tonic”, and foxglove, a tall plant with bright blossoms that “increases the activity of all forms of muscle and tissue, but more especially that of the heart,” are both considered common plants as well as medically potent (Grieve 354). Eliot writes in a period, however, where Silas’s knowledge is to become subcultural. The medicinal uses of such plants for example, was excluded from formal botanical knowledge, from books which Eliot owned like those by Ferdinand Jules Cohn which cover topics ranging from the connective tissues of plants to carnivorous plants (Baker 41). These texts are alongside a wide range of books and periodicals on the subjects of botany, plant WOMEN’S STUDIES 5

cultivation, and, most notably, a 16 volume run of Nature, a British scientific journal that, first published after the publication of Silas Marner, covered all contemporary scientific schools of thought including botany and medicine but treated old-fashioned herbs like those Silas collects as either weeds or flowers for growing in a domestic garden, depending on the beauty of the herb’s foliage (Baker lviii). In 1861, plant-based medicines were already giving way to patent medi­ cines and the more controlled and industrialized botany which Eliot’s library reflected. Knowledge of medicinal plants seemed old-fashioned despite their ongoing importance. Under laissez faire economics, moreover, herbs could be cheaply imported into England, and/or cultivation could be industrialized. Local herb gardens and foraging such as Marner’s was taken over by com­ mercial growers and importers (Sanecki 78). With licorice, lavender, and most culinary herbs coming from abroad or large commercial farms, domes­ tic gardens became decorative. Such gardening might be relegated to women “for fun” rather than for health (Sanecki 80). This gendered domestication and the resulting Victorian language of flowers as well as the “botanical vernacular” which linked flowers to women, obscures the ecological violence of this shift as the rise of a cult of flowers obscures the decline of the status of local medicinal plants in modernity and hence a decline in plant literacy and biodiversity (King). Eliot’s novel then not only describes the defoliation of culture in modernity, a concept defined by Randy Laist in which modern culture has plants and plant agency systematically stripped away until they are like foreign bodies, she prescribes it by replacing Silas’s womanly herbal­ ism with an apparently leafless, paternalist pharmaceutical industry as Silas himself, the feminized healer of the village, gives up his herbal medicine in order to participate in a modernized culture which, as was happening during the time that Eliot was writing, was focused on male-driven and formally educated pharmaceutical medicine (Laist 15). Indeed, while there was a history of men using plants to create medicine early in the nineteenth century, increasingly for the Victorians, botany and medicine parted ways; medicine was increasingly industrialized while plant cultivation in general was seen as the only scientific field considered “a genteel pastime for women” (Peterson 45). The connection to flowers and visually appealing plants gave botany an “elegant beauty” that caused it to be deemed a fittingly feminine pursuit (King 16). In many ways this rise in female botanists is due to the work of Carl Linnaeus. Linnaeus’ system of classifying plants was an inherently sexualized and often eroticized method of classifying and understanding plant reproduction. In his understanding of plants, flowers often marry one another, sometimes the reproduction of a species being explicitly erotic. Through this gendering of vegetal reproduc­ tion, Linnaeus provided Victorian culture with a socially acceptable means of discussing sex and sexuality. Women had the tools to discuss sexuality openly 6 C. ANDERSON

and explicitly in floral narratives. But Linnaeus also “explicitly included rather than excluded women from the study of botany” (King 17). Therefore, Linnaean botany opened the door to plants being a tool for women to speak more freely of their own bodies and sexuality, but also purposely included women in the study of plants. With the now scientific connections between the bloom of a young woman coming of age and the bloom of a growing flower, botany and the study of plants was not just something open to women but was something “morally improving” (King 16). Going out into both domestic gardens but also trekking into the wild­ erness to view, draw, paint, catalog, and study plants became a means of accomplishment for young Victorian women. Hence, plants, especially imported ones, still “helped late Victorian readers think about themselves and their world, in all its political, economic, and scientific expanses” (Chang 85). But for Victorians, herbs were not of much interest and medicinal plants were not the subject of botanical studies. Hence, a plant’s potency mattered little under the Linnaean system. If “herbs remained” the “remedies to be relied upon . . . for the country people” then “native and naturalized species were considered to be old fashioned” (Sanecki 70). The fear and apprehension as well as the magical belief that the villagers in Silas Marner display toward Silas’ work with plants, then, reflect an earlier time when herbs were taken quite seriously as a matter of life and death. The people of Raveloe, the village in which the majority of the novel takes place, even against Silas’s own admonitions, see Silas’ work as both necessary and helpful, and as dangerous witchcraft, an ideology that char­ acterizes them as “backward” or “primitive,” irrational and childlike. Eliot’s narrative of Silas’s “new self,” like the Victorian library, edits out the agency of plants in typically Victorian fashion. Existing outside books and scientific journals, Silas’ knowledge is vegetal and untamed. Hence, initially Silas’s plant knowledge inspires a “half-fearful fascination,” is rumored to be able to heal illnesses “if you could only speak the devil fair enough,” and is powerful enough to cure the villagers of their various ailments. At this point in the novel, herbs retain their potency, they are useful things in and of themselves, not to be put in print or translated into figures (Eliot 2, 3, 5). “Marner’s stuff” is powerful in its plant form itself, fashioned into a symbol and unfashionable. But this potency places the consumer in the role of Eve, speaking the Devil fair in return for what is perceived as sinister power. Herbal power Plants have a long history of being the source of what is sometimes con­ sidered a dangerous power, perhaps particularly when they are in the hands of a woman. There was a “fear of female power to deceive and destroy men” WOMEN’S STUDIES 7

that can be traced throughout much of British history as a misogynistic “footnote” to social philosophy and culture (Hallissy xi). This caused female apothecaries and medical practitioners during the Middle Ages to become known as veneficia. During this time period in England the apothecary was viewed as a man of science and medicine, a trusted healer for the community, while the venefica, or apothecary’s wife, was a figure of witchcraft and medicine. The female healer did not heal simply through science but through charms and potions she created using the herbs from her apothecary hus­ band. This stereotype was only compounded by the folk history of witchcraft connecting powerful women to the supernatural world. Therefore, “this belief in the possibility of supernatural aid reinforced the general belief in women as deceptive and therefore possibly poisoners. Since she who knows the drugs that heal must also know the drugs that kill, accepting a potion from a woman was a risky business” (Hallissy 63). Because Silas’ gender is made queer and unsteady through his feminized herbal knowledge, it makes sense that he is treated not as a masculine herbalist but as a feminine one. In order to see this connection, it becomes important to note that another term for this Medieval and Renaissance figure of the supernatural female healer is a Wise Woman. In Raveloe, the role that Silas fills is one “that had not been known since the Wise Woman at Tarley died” (Eliot 16). Literally placed into the role of the feminized healer, Silas finds himself “beset” by villagers looking to seek treatment of their own physical ills or those of their children (16). But their insistence that he can help them and their willingness to pay for his services does not mean the villagers are treating Silas with care and respect. Like a venefica, the villagers still view him as someone to be feared even as he is used for his medical abilities. Silas does not then enjoy his ability to use herbs. As a devout Christian, he not only “ha[s] doubts about the lawfulness” of his herbal knowledge, but also believes that “herbs could have no efficacy without prayer, and that prayer might suffice without the herbs” (7). In his mind, these “charms” as the villagers call them, are from an older religion, evil temptations in Silas’s eyes. The previous Wise Woman offered “little bags” to wear around the neck and would tie “a bit of red thread round [a] child’s toe” to prevent “water in the head” (16). This is what the villagers want from Silas. They want him to perform magic and they call his treat­ ments “stuff” and “charms,” which dilutes the reality that what he is provid­ ing is plant-based medicine. Being unwilling to chant and perform the charms that the villagers desire, both because he considers them a “falsity” and also because of his own moral discomfort with this supernatural and un-Christian practice, Silas sends the multitude of villagers away when they seek out his remedies (Eliot 16). His ability to treat the heart condition of Sally Oates, but refusal to continue to practice his medicine, gives him “a transient sense of brotherhood” which 8 C. ANDERSON

only “heightened the repulsion between him and his neighbors, and made his isolation more complete” (17). Blaming his “ill will and irritated glances” for any misfortune, as they assume him to have mystical power, Silas is isolated from the villagers (17). Though they viewed his medical abilities with a fearful fascination that leaves Silas othered, the villagers truly reject him from their society when he refuses to perform in the anachronistic and feminine role that they have set forth for him. Indeed, the villagers’ magical ideas of Silas’ work cast his herbal knowledge into the realm of belief rather than reason, magic rather than science. Silas dreads such associations and finds them a “temptation” he would prefer to avoid. If Silas Marner is a fable of entry into modernity, then neither plants nor their practices will be able to come forward into a more rational present. Eliot’s construction of the villagers’ ignorance and superstition, then, serves to defoli­ ate modern society, a literary deforestation that naturalizes the industrial practice. As the misguided community demands “charms,” Silas must logically refuse them (Eliot 5). “Marner’s stuff” that he provides is to them a “shadowy conception of power” instead of a rational medicine (7). The naming of it is reflective of this hazy, uncertain medicine that the novel depicts Marner as providing. It is not a cure. It is not a charm. Instead, it is merely “stuff:” an umbrella term for a tangible item that gives no insight into its origins or purpose and, as such, something which has an inherently disputable purpose as “stuff” is neither good nor bad by definition. The Oxford English Dictionary reflects this ambiguous definition, containing dozens of definitions of the word that range from tangible working items to intangible emotions. This serves to other Marner’s cures, separating them from both the supernatural and the medical so that the cures and the herbs they come from are relegated to an impotent and undesirable third classification of simply “stuff.” While herbs are still present in this text, their meaning is as contested as the definition of “stuff”. Ultimately plants are sacrificed to modernity despite the fact that Silas and his kin have real medical abilities. A plant like digitalis, for example, the medical name for foxglove, is powerful. It regulates the heartbeat and when used with skill in the novel it cures Sally Oates. Such plants provide Silas with the power to control his catalepsy and aid villagers, and should be powerful figures in this novel. But by emphasizing their cultural role as irrational charms, Eliot must then, seemingly logically or naturally, defoliate the novel for the villagers’ own good. Such an undomesticated person as Silas Marner is not a part of a modernized society and is, therefore, dangerous to the system. In order to ease the tensions of such socially necessary modernization, Silas must, inevi­ tably, become tamed and domesticated so that his “natural” knowledge becomes socially constructive. Following the gendered history of the garden in Victorian culture, herbs are relegated to women’s ornamental gardens, disempowering both “Marner’s stuff,” the bodies of plants themselves, and women. WOMEN’S STUDIES 9

Uprooting herbs in Victorian society Although Eliot makes the decline of herbalism seem a social good, histori­ cally, the rise of the industrial pharmaceutical complex meant a loss of access to and cultivation of medicinal plants like the ones Silas finds crowded with so many memories, the herbs themselves still present in the land as “it was only knowledge of herbs and plant literacy that had vanished” from the culture he is depicted living in (Carroll, New Woman Ecologies 153). The boom in farming developed monoculture in England. Gone were the sub­ sistence farms in which a family grew and knew medicinal plants, which either died out through the selling of land or through the same farmers buying up more and more land in order to create a commercial farm (Eliot 11). Land that had previously been untouched was snatched up and parceled out for commercial farming, pushing domestic plants further away from civilized spaces. With less space available, plants had to compete with one another for the space to grow, limiting biodiversity with the limitations on untouched “wild” spaces. Silas Marner obscures the violence of a defoliation which occurred at multiple levels: in farming, in medicine, and in literature and culture. The farming villages in Silas Marner remain populated with people and now unused plants. In Raveloe, the seat of power is not business but Squire Cass who is one of “several landed parishioners” (Eliot 20). Early in the novel we learn of the soft rhythm of farming present in the novel that is characterized by the “cheerful trotting of the winnowing machine” (2). Any tension between the old way of doing things and new values is ultimately smoothed over in the figure of Silas Marner himself. One of the first things learned about Silas is that he is a weaver. Silas’ loom is iconic of his profession of weaving fine cloth from “flaxen thread” and linen made from flax (1). As this is the early years of the nineteenth century, it takes place before the Luddite rebellion which began in 1811 (2). The movement, a rebellion of radical textile workers who protested the growing textile mills as well as the horrible conditions in the mills, marked a shift in textile production from the individual artisan to factories of mass production. Consequently, a weaver such as Silas would not be an unusual sight, even if his presence is still seen as “other” from the community. His work, the day- to-day toiling that he does, links him to plants immediately. Flax is spun from plant fibers and so even before the text introduces his medical herbal knowledge, Silas is tied to plant life. He spends his days “bent close down on the slow growth” of his weaving, the thread passing through his fingers and past his eyes as he creates his cloth (19). Even in his weaving his eyes and his hands are constantly touching and dealing with plant-based thread. But for a man at the start of the nineteenth century, such close proximity to plants was not unnatural or unusual. This intimacy with plant fibers is not only 10 C. ANDERSON

acceptable but admired in mid-nineteenth-century British culture. However, the socially understood masculine profession of textiles was, during this time, ceasing to be produced by a single man in his house like Silas, and was shifting to an industrialized production. We can see this shift in the slight othering of Silas. When Silas acts as an herbalist he is feared and related to a practitioner of the supernatural by a town which can be read to represent the modernization of British society. When Silas weaves he is not shunned, merely seen as an outsider. He is not the fully modernized textile industry worker, but he is also acting in a profession that still existed and was admired. In this way he becomes a site of modernization wherein “archaic” herbalism is shunned, but his literal cottage industry weaving is more odd than industrialized weaving is but is still a socially acceptable interaction with plants via their fibers. Although the production of linen from flax was not the most popular fabric as “favor was shown toward the wool industry,” the weaving of flaxen thread had still been significant since the late sixteenth century (Wilson 15). By the time Eliot was writing, though, the “old cottage industry was displaced by a factory system” (Wilson 16). Returning to the idea that Silas’ loom sounds disturbing when compared to the “natural cheerful trotting of the winnowing machine,” Eliot’s depiction of Silas works to denaturalize artisa­ nal weaving and gives favor to industrialization (Eliot 2). The sounds of machinery, though not machines associated with industrial textile factories, sound “natural” and are associated with pleasant emotions. Silas, on the other hand, is such an unknown and othered figure that he is “alien-looking” and represents a strange and “disinherited” profession that has been left behind by society (1). Mid-nineteenth-century society had shifted to favoring the wool and cotton fabrics that industrial textile mills produced easily and cheaply over the labor-intensive work of hand-woven flax, and so even though they live at the start of the nineteenth century, the villagers display disdain for Silas’ archaic profession. The impact this shift had on plants cannot be ignored, either. Flax is both a food product and a source of natural fibers. As such, it lent itself well to preindustrial societies as farmers could sell the waste from their flax harvest to a weaver who could then turn it into flaxen thread and linens. This fabric was replaced by wool and cotton, both of which required large plots of land to be domesticated and dedicated either to sheep or to the farming of cotton. The attitude of the villagers reflects mid- nineteenth-century society in which the undomesticated “natural” world continued to be pushed further back by expanding cities and growing commercial farms. Silas’ cures are frightening even as the villagers seek them out, craving his supernatural healing. Just as textile production industrialized during the nineteenth century, so too did medicine. Upset with doctors like Doctor Kimble, Raveloe’s resident physician who had very little training and even WOMEN’S STUDIES 11

less regulation, British medicine was “crumbling under the weight of practi­ tioners’ discontents” (Peterson 283). These discontent patients, failed by a medical field with little regulation and poorly educated medical practi­ tioners who sometimes harmed more than they helped, led to the litigation and standardization of the medical field in England. Starting with the Apothecaries Act of 1815 and culminating in the creation of a General Practitioner (GP) position that could be studied at hospitals, medicine spent the nineteenth century shifting away from the cures of an apothecary and toward the lab-refined tablets of a GP. The movement toward regulation and requirements concerning the training of doctors, as well as medical breakthroughs such as the invention of the stethoscope in 1816, anesthesia in 1842, and antiseptic surgical practices in 1862, led to a medical renais­ sance. This influx of knowledge came with a price, though. In order to mass- produce medicine, labs had to distil reagents into easily produced and easily prescribed forms so that the medical field could become standardized and modernized. An herbalist like Silas had no place in the industrialization of medicine. And so, even though the novel takes place before this shift in cultural conceptions of medicine, Silas’ herbal cures are seen as illegitimate and potentially sinister witchcraft which is better connected to archaic beliefs about Wise Women than to legitimate medicine. The plants themselves suffer for this loss of medical connection just as Silas does. Two of the three plants Silas is explicitly stated as using, dandelion and coltsfoot, are common herbs used in remedies for common ailments. Both plants also have deep and sturdy roots that allow them to flourish in virtually any terrain in England. And for both of these plants, that ability to grow well has garnered them the title of “weed.” They became considered invasive and were plucked out of the ground and kept away from domestic spaces as the domestic garden gained popularity during the nineteenth century. Garden plants were chosen carefully to be a beautiful and sweet- smelling display (Sanecki 72). Little attention was paid to the impact this had on plants outside of the domestic garden and, in some cases, this led to invasive species like the Japanese knotweed being planted. First introduced to England around the middle of the nineteenth century because of its beauty, the Japanese knotweed became such an invasive species and proved to be so adept at choking out domestic plants, that the proliferation of the plant became illegal in England in the twentieth century. But Victorian gardeners did not care about invasive species or whether or not they were harming plants in their selective breeding for larger, fuller blossoms. Instead, their gardens served as displays of beauty and the personality of the home, much like Eppie’s own garden does later in the novel. Silas must be brought into line with this modern vegetal world. He must give up his plants for something socially “natural.” This is something he seems to struggle with at first as his queer connection with plants initially 12 C. ANDERSON

shifts to a queer obsession with gold. Eliot classifies plants with metals, shifting Silas’s desire to touch and know from plants and gold to people. The things that were once his family when he “handled them” and “counted them, till their form and colour were like the satisfaction of a thirst for him,” were once “companionship,” as Nunokawa says, a stand in for masturbation or sexual intimacy, queered because it lies outside heteronormative repro­ duction (17). The intimacy he shared with plants through their connection to his mother and his wanderings to collect them is now focused on the coins, keeping his expressions of intimacy and nigh sexual thirst focused wholly on inanimate objects. He remains queer and the society continues to treat him as such. When his coins are stolen it marks for Silas the first time he has truly been a part of the community. Eliot says that the support and attention of the villagers “had doubtless its influence on Marner, in spite of his passionate preoccupation with his loss” (Eliot 56). This affection changes Silas and changes what he values in life. Upon finding little Eppie in his house and mistaking her golden hair for his golden coins, Silas adopts her and takes on the responsibility of raising her himself. She becomes his “precious plant to which he would give a nurturing home in a new soil” and in turn he will have to rely on society to “help him to satisfy the wants of the searching roots” (Eliot 136). For the first time since coming to the village of Raveloe, Silas is expressing desire and intimacy toward another human. It is not a sexual desire, but it is still enough to seemingly rectify his queerness. A child is a product of a socially accep­ table heterosexual relationship. It stands to reason that his affection for a child, even without the presence of a female sexual partner for him to desire, moves him away from his queer passions for plants and gold and focuses his intimacy on something more socially acceptable. Plants become only the “stuff” of metaphor rather than vibrant matter. What was before represented as a potent medicinal herb, used to treat medical conditions, is now domesticated. Silas too is replanted in domesticated soil through the adoption of Eppie. He no longer desires gold. He is no longer isolated from the village. There is a “softening of feeling towards him” among the villagers that leads the women in the village, in particular his neighbor Dolly Winthrop, to provide him with clothes for Eppie and assistance in sorting out how to raise her as a single father. Now domesticated, Silas is freed from the “cold, narrow prison” he was once held in (131). In the novel, it is nothing but a good thing that Silas turns his back on what was once his passion in order to fall in line with social expectations of domestication and procreation. This domestication still involves a potential queering, though. Silas is to be Eppie’s only parent. While he takes advice from Dolly Winthrop, he serves as both mother and father to the little girl. Yet the previously present othering in which the village was drawn to Silas even as they rejected him is not WOMEN’S STUDIES 13

present. Therefore, it must be the plants themselves that are negative and harmful to his soul, and not the connection to femininity. Plants seem to surround Eppie at all times and she is Silas’ metaphorical plant which he must give tender care and attention to in order to satisfy his own soul. In return, Eppie brings Silas into society by giving him a positive outlet for his gender and overshadowing any lingering queerness in his person. While Eppie, and her garden once she is grown, serve to repeat and confirm more modernized Victorian views of plants, her presence is initially a disruptive one. As Eppie conforms to social standards and brings Silas into the modernized fold, Silas’s adoption of Eppie immediately disrupts his foraging and his intimacy with plants so that he is able to redefine his relationship with the vegetal world. While out walking with Eppie when she is still a toddler, “Silas began to look for the once-familiar herbs” he used to walk the fields in search of (Eliot 131). It is clear that these plants are no longer familiar tools of his trade. He truly has let that part of his life go. Nostalgia for plants replaces intimacy and knowledge, plant literacy itself. The things themselves must be left behind. Eliot says, “as the leaves, with their unchanged outline and markings, lay on his palm, there was a sense of crowding remembrances from which he turned away timidly” (131). These “once-familiar” plants must be “turned away” though they may still be the “temptation” he once saw them as (131, 7). Parting in sorrow, he holds the leaves in his hands and recognizes their outline and markings. These plant bodies were once his only contact with living things, accentuated by the fact that Silas had certainly no intention of marrying once he arrived in Raveloe. While he has interest in a woman early in the novel, the only human intimacy that we see Silas have is the familial intimacy he has with his adopted daughter, Eppie. The focus on touch and the feeling of these plants on Silas’ palm feels markedly intimate. The “crowding remembrances,” a dense population of memories all rushing back to him at the touch of these leaves, move Silas into close proximity with the plants he is touching. These leaves have enough power and agency to affect Silas’ sexuality. While this scene is not an explicitly sexual one, it is an intimate and haptic scene. In a book where Silas’ touch carries a great deal of weight, the folding of his coins transferring to his penchant for folding Eppie’s golden curls, his fondling of the leaves in this scene suggests a queerness of sexuality that is not dependent on hetero- or homosexuality. Instead, his touching of the plants is an expression of sexuality and close intimacy. Like the obsession with his coins, this intimate touching of plants is an improper expression of desire for Silas and, therefore, is redirected. He is only content when he expresses affection and parental desire toward Eppie. Eppie, however, is not only allowed to be connected to the “natural” world, but her connection is supported and rewarded. Flowers, a tool for healing at the start of the novel, are now playthings for Eppie as she “toddled to pluck 14 C. ANDERSON

the flowers” (Eliot 130). The image of “buttercups . . . thick in the meadows” is used to indicate the passing of time and the blooming in Silas’ life thanks to Eppie, but they are also a metaphor or a set dressing for her development (130). The meadow of buttercups does nothing. It does not provide healing and it does not even seem to provide smell or pollen for the bees. The activity and life of the vegetal world is entirely missing. Much like Eppie plucking the flowers, Eliot has plucked the flowers, thus separating them from their roots and the source of their life so that the novel is left with one-dimensional plants which are present but inactive. These inert plants are accepted and loved while the “once-familiar herbs” are something that Silas “turn[s] away timidly” from when he sees them (131). The language used here is notable. The buttercups are “thick” in the meadow, but that is the only descriptor of the inert and positively presented plants. But the medicinal herbs are sur­ rounded by various negative descriptors, thus marking their active presence in the story as negative. Their memories are “crowding,” eliciting a sense of uncomfortable anxiety due to the packed-in memories (130). Looking at them, Silas’ spirit is “enfeebled” and when he turns away it is “timidly” (130). Silas becomes passive and weak after only holding these plants in his hand. Plant fondling, it seems, is now strictly prohibited. Such queer touch­ ing should be replaced as Silas takes “refuge in Eppie’s little world”; his attention to Eppie, which has been previously called perverse, becomes his only tie to a socially acceptable and modernized world. This fearful reaction is aligned with the changing social climate toward plants in modernity. The plants that were once his potent allies he now turns away from like a fearful lover, their touch and their potency now frightening to him in his moder­ nized worldview. These plants are, now, only comforting when contained within the domestic space of the garden. Eppie’s garden The final moment of defoliation in Silas Marner comes then when plants are domesticated and feminized through their placement in Eppie’s garden. Eppie, associated with plants since her entry into the novel as she “toddle[s] to pluck the flowers” and is to Silas “a precious plant to which he would give a nurturing home,” transfers Silas’s nurturing energies from plants to par­ enthood (Eliot 130, 136). She is ultimately the flower Silas grows and expresses the disciplining of plants and her proper femininity by containing both within the space of her garden at the end of the novel. Like the gardens of female botanists during the nineteenth century, Eppie’s garden is a positive place for her to contain her desires. One of the first things she desires when she asks for a garden is “double daises” (141). Double daises are daisies which were carefully and selectively bred to have extra petals in their bloom, creating a flower which has upwards of twice as many petals as a naturally WOMEN’S STUDIES 15

occurring daisy. These double daisies being chosen first is representative of the kinds of flowers and plants which were acceptable in this modernized society: flowers which had been shaped and altered by humans so that they no longer truly resembled their wild cousins. Like the double daisies, the plants Eppie wants in her garden are chosen to increase social standing or are inert. The double daisies are “like Mrs. Winthrop’s” and the list of herbs she wishes to include, rosemary, bergamot, and thyme, are chosen because they are “sweet-smelling,” and yet lavender, a plant so desired by Victorians that commercial farmers grew it, is omitted because “there’s no lavender only in the gentlefolks’ gardens” (142). Eppie selects plants for her garden based mostly on social pressure, here. The “sweet-smelling” herbs allow her to produce potpourri or nosegays, both popular in Victorian homes, while the double daisies mirror Mrs. Winthrop and lavender is omitted because it isn’t what gentlefolks grow in their garden (Eliot 154). While lavender does appear in the novel, it is the scent of lavender that “fills the vases” in houses rather than gardens (154). The flowers, too, are not chosen for any purpose but to be beautiful and inert. Eppie says she wants to plant flowers because “[she] always think[s] the flowers can see us and know what we’re talking about” (142). While this may seem like a moment of vegetal presence in the novel, it reveals her desire for a living but inert garden. These are not the herbs Silas used to use, chosen for their activity in the body and ability to heal. These are flowers chosen so they can be passive viewers of the household, beautiful and sweet-smelling, but only able to exist and grow. The closest they come to affecting the world around them is the social status that society has placed on some plants over others. Eppie is affected by plants in this way as her femininity and domestic identity are defined by her garden. If “the bloom of a girl [is] like the bloom of a plant,” then Eppie fully blooms into a woman when she asks her father for a garden (King 35). Whereas Silas’ sexuality and gender are initially presented as queer, Eppie’s is consistently in line with the social norm. She grows into a beautiful young woman who is interested in a local gardener, Aaron. Considering the metaphor of flowers as a “description of a potential and ephemeral sexual reproduction,” the connection between Aaron’s pro­ fession and Eppie’s sudden desire to plant a garden reveals a desire for her sexuality to bloom under the caretaking of Aaron. This is a socially accep­ table and correct way to express her sexuality. Because Linnaean botany used the readily available and conceptually accessible tools of gender in order to describe plant reproduction, within society “sex became spoken” through the language of blooms and flowers (King 13). Flowers had sexual organs under Linnaean distinctions and discussions of a beautiful bloom or floral repro­ duction were coded language that could be used to openly discuss a woman’s sexuality or sex itself. As if they are building her womb in which she will bear 16 C. ANDERSON

their children, Aaron and Eppie build Eppie’s garden under the watchful eye of Silas. In a culmination of Eliot’s modernization of Silas and the novel, Eppie ends as the perfectly modernized Victorian woman. She does not fret over the changing water in the stone pit due to larger farms requiring more irrigation water. She does not wander through the woods. She has not inherited Silas’ knowledge of medicinal herbs. She is a domesticated beauty who is married off young and who has “a larger garden than she had ever expected” (187). She is fertile and blooms sexually through the metaphor of her blooming garden, thus being perfectly appropriate and perfectly domes­ ticated. Even though the novel ends filled with plant life, it is newly inert, a metaphorical stand-in for humanity and sexuality. This lush garden at the end of the novel, though beautiful, is powerless and domesticated and so represents a defoliation of the few wild, powerful, and narratively present herbs Silas gathers at the start of it. In the same way that the villagers shunning Silas’ knowledge of medicinal herbs, an act anachronistic for early nineteenth-century rural communities which heavily relied on herbal medicine, exposes a desire to eschew tradi­ tional medicine as archaic representations of pagan beliefs in favor of a naturalized and industrialized medicine and society, so too does this oxymoron of a defoliated garden expose the social realities of the time in which George Eliot was writing. During the nineteenth century, medicine moved away from its herbal roots. While the purely scientific side of Victorian botany focused on discovering and cataloging plants, the popular culture side of botany saw a boom in superficiality. Plants became tools to create beauty and decorate a home. While flowers and plants were often everywhere, they were manipulated and controlled so they represented not their own vegetal beauty and power, but the beauty and meaning that humanity desired. It is this control of plants that can be seen in George Eliot’s Silas Marner. The plants with real power are treated as terrifying agents of a supernatural power while the second half of the novel has lush vegetation, but with an inert, one-dimensional life whose only purpose is to amplify the humans present or serve as a sexual metaphor. It is foliated but it is not planted with vegetal life and power, displaying a balance between man and nature. Instead, it is planted in such a way that reifies humanity as above and superior to plants, creating vegetation that does not reflect vegetal life but instead only reflects the nearby human presence. In the industrialized Victorian society of the mid-nineteenth century when George Eliot was writing Silas Marner, such a view of flowers and gardens was the modernized one to have. Considering the treatment of Silas and his knowledge of medicinal herbs, it becomes apparent that this novel is pushing toward an easy-to-accept and peaceful modernization through industry. It is seen in Eppie’s garden. It is seen as the stone pit has less and less water, the flow being diverted to help farms which grew larger as industry advanced. WOMEN’S STUDIES 17

The evidence of industry is taken even further at the end of the novel when Silas and Eppie return to Lantern Yard. Rather than finding the church at the center of town, they find “a large factory, from which men and women were streaming for their midday meal” (Eliot 183). The village from the start of the novel is gone, replaced by a factory, a literal embodiment of industry. Such a sight in what was a peaceful and seemingly idyllic farming community should be deeply unsettling. While both Silas and Eppie express discomfort and surprise at the former village of Lantern Yard, the story quickly diverts away from the place and back onto the happiness that Silas and Eppie have found together. As if brushing upon the fact that industry inherently changes the countryside, Eliot draws the reader back into the comforting reality that Silas and Eppie are perfectly happy as Eppie closes the novel out by saying, “I think nobody could be happier than we are” (187). Any discomfort or violence is obscured by the social systems. Any hardships are forgotten because the characters have found happiness in their family home. Eliot’s Silas Marner charts the expulsion of plants from medicine and the split between the latter and botany which was a field which was increasingly gendered as female and amateur. Plants shift from active things, queering Silas’ gender and sexual expression while carrying both memory and healing properties, to inert symbols, becoming statements of social status in Eppie’s garden or literal wallflowers who can only observe but never interact. Eliot seems to work hard to assuage any fears of modernization, discrediting old ways of thinking as worthy of the Middle Ages and enough to cause someone to be a social outcast. While Eliot defoliates the landscape of Silas Marner of local food and potent local medicinal plants, she also plants a troubling new kind of garden that naturalizes modernity and women’s place in it. Neither Silas nor Eppie can find true happiness until they eradicate potent plants. By containing them in the space of the domestic garden, plants become docile and “naturalized” in the modernity of society. Growing changes in Victorian culture In the novel, Eliot applies pressure to the vibrant matter of plants, shifting them from the literal to the figurative realm (Bennett vii). The traditional practice of herbal healing is exiled and linked to magic as well as the realm of the irrational, while potent local plants themselves are shown to their proper place, becoming mere signs of the decorative and feminine, rather than a utilitarian one, a woman’s place on the margins of culture. Even while medicinal plants are still present, then, seeming to foliate the pages of the novel, potent plants have been stripped away and replaced with inert metaphorical stand-ins. The result of Silas’ domestication is clear in Eppie’s decorative garden which ironically predicts the rise of a gendered language of flowers and the defoliation of the English novel, the seemingly 18 C. ANDERSON

proper and natural rise of the consumption of biomedicine rather than plant-based medicine. Increasingly, queer outliers like Silas are aligned with the heterosexual family and the concomitant decline of biodiversity literacy. Silas’ queerness is built on multiple aspects of his personality, his habits, history, and actions working together to build a queer figure in the novel. Jeff Nunokawa famously connects Silas’ illicit pleasure in touching his coins alone at night with his shutters closed to a “condensed catalogue of sexual deviance” in which the coins he earned are fondled in an act of incestuous masturbation (274). He is made queer through his rejection of the traditional social and sexual familial structures, choosing to not gain pleasure from a woman but, instead, from the coins he produced through the work of his own body. Nunokawa suggests this sexual deviance borders on connections with homosexuality or the behaviors of a “sodomite,” and that Eliot reaffirms the traditional family by having Silas’ salvation come in the form of an altered yet still traditional family as he parents Eppie and his “perversity is dispelled” (274, 289). Silas’ parenting, though, is still a deviation from the socio-sexual landscape that Eliot wrote in and wrote about. Adopting Eppie, Silas has gained a child without sexual reproduction and, in doing so, steps into the genderless role of both mother and father to Eppie, caring for her and guiding her as a sole parent. In an act of almost parthenogenesis, Silas has a child. Of course, Silas does not literally reproduce asexually or become a female, but metaphorically within the novel, his gender and sexuality are unseated and left without much definition as his self-love of coins leads to the production of a child when his love for gold leads to him taking in Eppie and raising her as his own child, her golden curls reminding Silas of his stolen hoard of coins and easing the sorrow the loss of the coins brought him. Notably, this all happens without a need for gender roles. Silas’ sexuality and gender cannot be defined simply by a binary. Because “binaries look suspiciously like covert extensions of the series ‘good/bad,’ in which one term is always defining one while the other is derivative,” I suggest an understanding of Silas’ queerness that looks to his influences and prefer­ ences rather than the set roles of a nineteenth-century man or woman (Wilchins 40). As contemporary queer theory begins to understand that “queer wants to subvert identity and have it too” by being the subversive “other” that is also collected enough to build personal and social identities around the concept of queerness, Silas can be read to be queer in the way he wants to subvert social expectations but be a part of society, too (Penney 11). He aligns himself with himself and his lineage through his masturbatory gold obsession and his matrilineal herbal knowledge defines him early in the novel as Silas chooses to end his family line in order to focus on these self- pleasuring acts. Divergent from society, Silas subverts expectations through finding self-identification through his mother, his gender unseated as he WOMEN’S STUDIES 19

becomes a healer like she was, and his sexual self-identification through the pleasure he finds in fondling his gold. George Eliot is described as a realist who created “images [that] are as much a part of the consciousness of the characters as representations of material reality” (Shuttleworth 9). Silas Marner reflects and constructs the Victorian “common sense” which pushed medicinal plants to the margins. It is only when Silas gives up his improper desires for the acceptable desire for a child, heteronormative and reproductive even as Silas serves as Eppie’s mother and father, that he finds peace and happiness at last. For women, plants were brought closer, but only the specific plants they were allowed to care for, were in fashion, or could be used to help define their blooming femininity. Eppie’s garden is the locus in which she becomes a woman and finds a husband with whom to procreate. There was no partnership between humanity and vegetal life and the vegetal life, while not at risk of immediate extinction, was not considered and often actively harmed in order to make room for industry, science, progress, and exotic species. George Eliot’s interpretation of plants in Silas Marner naturalizes this historical shift.
